summary: Defines new signaling messages and sub-options so a Mobile IPv6 home agent can initiate flow binding, such as moving a flow between access networks. It is experimental and supports IPv4 and IPv6 mobile nodes.

eli5.summary: The home base can tell your phone to switch which road a stream uses.

subtitle: Home agents can now tell mobile devices to move traffic streams between networks in real time, for load balancing and quality of service.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 lets devices keep working when they move networks, but it treats all traffic from a device the same way. A home agent (the base station managing the device) cannot push a decision to move video traffic to Wi-Fi when the cellular network is congested, or to shift voice calls to a more reliable path.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7109 adds new messages (Flow Binding Indication and Acknowledgement) that let the home agent request a mobile device to bind specific traffic flows to different networks. The device confirms or objects, then updates its local routing accordingly.
tldr.outcome: Mobile networks can now respond in real time to congestion, service policies, and emergencies by instructing devices to move streams without dropping them—video to Wi-Fi, voice to LTE, or best-effort traffic off the network entirely.

facts.label: Flow Binding operations
facts.value: Six: Add, Delete, Modify, Move, Refresh, Revoke

today: RFC 7109 is an Experimental specification published in February 2014. It has not been updated, obsoleted, or promoted to Standards Track. It remains in use in research networks and vendor implementations as a way for mobile operators to manage traffic at the home agent level. The specification has not seen widespread deployment, likely because many carriers use simpler traffic management techniques (policy servers, subscriber data repositories) rather than direct home agent initiated messages.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (RFC 6275) allows a mobile device to maintain its network identity (home address) as it moves between access networks, so sessions do not break when the device switches from cellular to Wi-Fi. Flow bindings, defined in RFC 6089, extend this: they let a device bind specific traffic flows (identified by IP addresses, ports, or protocols) to different care-of addresses (the device's actual addresses on each network). This way, video can go out one interface while voice goes out another.

RFC 6089 allows the mobile device to initiate all these bindings: the device decides which flows to move and when. This is fine when the device's software makes those decisions, but modern networks need to respond to conditions the home agent sees: congestion on a carrier network, changes in QoS policy, emergencies, or data-cap enforcement. RFC 7109 adds the missing direction: home agent initiated flow bindings. Now the home agent can tell a device 'Move this flow to a different interface,' and the device can respond with an acknowledgement and take action.
sections.eli5: Before, only the phone could decide to move its own traffic. Now the home base can also say 'I see you're congested; move X to Wi-Fi.' The phone checks if it can and replies. If yes, it shifts the traffic.

sections.title: Network Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC outlines four classes of scenarios where home agent control over flows is valuable. QoS provisioning is when the network wants to give different treatments to different flows: a video call needs more bandwidth and lower latency than an email client, so the network can ask the device to split them into separate flows with separate QoS settings. Traffic offload from congestion is when a mobile carrier wants to move non-critical flows from its congested 3G/LTE network to Wi-Fi to free capacity for critical services. Emergency situations (earthquakes, floods) may require the network to shut down non-critical services like gaming to save radio resources for emergency calls. Service-specific data caps allow the carrier to tell a device 'You have 5 GB for streaming video; shift it to a different interface if you want to keep using your unlimited voice service.'

In all cases, the home agent has visibility and policy that the device lacks. The device may not know the network is congested, may not know the operator's policy, or may not know there is an emergency. By adding home agent initiated flows, RFC 7109 gives the operator tools for fine-grained, real-time traffic management without requiring the device to be aware of network conditions.
sections.eli5: Reasons the home base might want to move a flow: the network is slow, the rules change, it's an emergency, or the user hit their data limit. The device does not see these things, so the base asks it nicely to move traffic around.

sections.title: Protocol Operations
sections.content:
When the home agent wants to manage a flow, it sends the device a Flow Binding Indication (FBI) message containing one or more flow identifiers and instructions on what to do. The device responds with a Flow Binding Acknowledgement (FBA). The RFC specifies six operation types that can be sent in an FBI. Add tells the device to split off a specific flow to a new interface. Delete removes a previously established binding. Modify changes the properties of an existing binding (for example, new QoS parameters). Refresh extends the lifetime of a binding before it expires. Move transfers a flow from one interface to another. Revoke tells the device the home agent is taking back a binding and the device should either delete it or move it elsewhere.

Each FBI contains a flow identifier (FID) and a traffic selector specifying which packets match the flow. In the case of a Move operation, a new sub-option called Target Care-of Address tells the device which interface to move the flow to. A Flow Binding Action sub-option indicates which operation to perform (add, delete, etc.). After an FBI/FBA exchange, the device MUST send a standard Mobile IPv6 Binding Update (BU) message to confirm the change in its binding cache at the home agent.
sections.eli5: The home base sends a message saying 'Move flow #3 to your other interface' or 'Delete flow #2.' The device says 'OK' or 'I can't; I don't have that interface anymore.' Then the device sends its own message to lock in the change if it said yes.

sections.title: Messages and Mobility Options
sections.content:
The new messages defined in this RFC use the Mobile IPv6 Mobility Header format (Section 6.1 of RFC 6275). The Flow Binding Indication has a message type value of 21 and includes a sequence number (to correlate with responses), a trigger field (indicating the reason for the request, such as 'administrative reason' or 'out-of-sync'), and an Acknowledge flag. It carries zero or more Flow Identification Mobility options defining which flows to operate on.

The Flow Binding Acknowledgement also uses message type 21 but has a different type subfield. It echoes the sequence number and includes a status field: status 0 means success, status 128 or higher indicates failure (for example, status 128 means the target care-of address does not exist). Two new sub-options extend the Flow Identification option: the Flow Binding Action sub-option (type 4) specifies the operation (add, delete, move, etc.), and the Target Care-of Address sub-option (type 5) specifies which interface to move the flow to (required only for Move operations).

The home agent retransmits the FBI up to three times (by default) if no FBA is received within 3 seconds. If the device does not support Flow Binding messages, it responds with a Binding Error message, and the home agent knows not to send FBI messages to that device again.
sections.eli5: The messages are fairly simple: a header with a sequence number and trigger reason, a list of flows to operate on, and the action to take. The device sends back a confirmation message with a status code (success or a specific failure reason).

sections.title: Deployment and Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 7109 explicitly supports both IPv6-only and dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) deployments. Devices with both IPv4 and IPv6 home addresses can have flows bound to either address family independently. The document also addresses corner cases: if the device's network conditions change and an interface the home agent targets becomes unavailable, the home agent will not receive an FBA and will learn to stop using that interface. If a device roams between networks and NAT/firewall conditions change, existing NAT keepalive mechanisms from RFC 5555 handle the situation.

Flow binding operations update a flow bindings list at the home agent. When an operation succeeds, the home agent adds, removes, or modifies an entry in its internal list. The list tracks which flows are bound to which interfaces and which ones are active. This list persists across multiple FBI/FBA exchanges, so the home agent can later refresh, modify, or revoke bindings it issued in the past.

The RFC notes that this specification is for home agent initiated operations only; the device can still initiate its own flow binding updates using the mechanisms in RFC 6089. Both sides can manage flows, but only the home agent can proactively push changes in this RFC's model.
sections.eli5: Phones with both IPv4 and IPv6 work fine. The home base keeps a list of which flows are bound where. If something changes on the phone's side and it can't follow an order, it just says no. And the phone can still initiate its own moves too; the home base doesn't have absolute control.

sections.title: Security and Standards Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 7109 inherits the security model from RFC 6089 (flow bindings), RFC 6088 (traffic selectors), and RFC 5846 (binding revocation). All Mobile IPv6 messages are authenticated using the IPsec security association between the device and home agent, so a home agent cannot send an FBI that appears to come from a different source. The home agent can only manage flow bindings that are already registered in its binding cache for that device; it cannot create bindings for arbitrary addresses.

The document specifically allows the home agent to revoke bindings using the Binding Revocation message (from RFC 5846), which is a more forceful mechanism than deletion: a revocation can happen without the device's permission, whereas a deletion operation expects the device's acknowledgement. This mirrors the security model where the home agent is the authority for that device's bindings.

One security consideration the RFC notes is that the home agent MUST handle retransmission carefully: if it retransmits an FBI and the device has already acted on it, reapplying the operation could cause unintended behavior. To prevent this, the sequence number in the FBI allows the device to recognize retransmissions and ignore duplicates.
sections.eli5: The phone and home base already trust each other with encryption. The home base can only control flows that are already registered. Revoking a flow is more forceful than asking to delete it. And the sequence number prevents the home base from accidentally doing the same thing twice if it has to resend a message.
